content_html:
Your credit card minimum payment is set by a formula, and because it is tied to the balance it falls as the balance falls. That sounds helpful, but it means each payment chips away less and less, so a card paid only at the minimum can take well over a decade to clear. This calculator applies your card's minimum payment formula month by month to show how long that takes, what it costs and how much a fixed payment would save.

How to use this calculator

  1. Card balance and APR: the amount you owe and the purchase rate from your latest statement.
  2. How your card sets the minimum: many large US issuers use the interest charged that month plus a small percentage of the balance (often 1%). Some cards use a flat percentage of the balance instead, commonly 2% to 4%.
  3. Percentage of balance and minimum dollar amount: the minimum due is whichever is larger, the formula or the dollar floor. If you owe less than the floor, the minimum is the full balance.
  4. More options: enter a fixed payment to compare against, and a payoff goal in months to see the payment that would clear the card in that time.

How the minimum payment is calculated

Each month the calculator charges interest at the APR divided by 12, which gives the statement balance. It then works out the minimum:

  • Interest plus a percentage: minimum = that month's interest + the percentage × the statement balance.
  • Percentage only: minimum = the percentage × the statement balance.

The result is compared with the dollar floor, the larger amount is paid, and the process repeats until the balance reaches zero. No new purchases are added. A percentage-only minimum that is lower than the monthly interest rate never reduces the balance; the calculator tells you when that happens.

A worked example

Take a $5,000 balance at 22% APR on a card whose minimum is interest plus 1%, with a $35 floor. The first month's interest is $91.67, so the statement balance is $5,091.67 and the minimum is $91.67 + $50.92 = $142.59. Paying only the minimum, the card takes 194 payments (16 years 2 months) to clear and costs $7,548.41 in interest, more than the original balance.

If you kept paying that first $142.59 every month instead of letting the payment shrink, the card would be paid off in 4 years 9 months with $3,081.60 of interest. Raising the payment to $190.96 clears it in 3 years with $1,874.14 of interest.

A low flat percentage is the most expensive formula by far: at 2% of the balance and a 22% APR, almost the whole payment goes to interest, so the balance barely moves until the dollar floor takes over.

Ways to get out of the minimum payment trap

  • Fix your payment. Pick an amount, even just your current minimum, and keep paying it as the balance falls. The comparison table shows how much this alone saves.
  • Read the disclosure on your statement. US card statements show how long minimum payments would take and the payment needed to pay off the balance in three years. This calculator lets you test other amounts and rates.
  • Stop new charges on the card. This calculator assumes no new purchases. Any new spending pushes the payoff date further out.
  • Look at the rate. A lower APR, from a hardship program or a balance transfer, shortens payoff even at the same minimum formula.

Results are estimates. Issuers charge interest on the average daily balance, may round the minimum to whole dollars and can add late fees or past-due amounts to the minimum.

faq.question: Why does my minimum payment keep going down?
faq.answer: The minimum is calculated from the balance, so each time the balance drops the next minimum is smaller. That keeps the payment affordable but means less goes toward the debt each month, which stretches repayment out for years.

faq.question: What happens if I pay less than the minimum?
faq.answer: Paying less than the minimum usually triggers a late fee, can lead to a penalty APR and may be reported to the credit bureaus if the payment is 30 or more days late. Always pay at least the minimum if you can.

faq.question: Is paying the minimum bad for my credit score?
faq.answer: Paying the minimum on time counts as an on-time payment. The bigger credit effect comes from the balance itself: a high balance relative to your limit raises your credit utilization, which can lower your score until it is paid down.

faq.question: Where do I find my card's minimum payment formula?
faq.answer: It is in your cardholder agreement, usually in the section on payments, and many issuers summarize it on their website or the back of the statement. If you cannot find it, interest plus 1% of the balance with a floor of around $25 to $40 is a common setup.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
